title: Bookkeeping Services for Small Businesses | 2ndCFO
description: Bookkeeping for small businesses in Redmond and the Seattle area. Reconciliations, monthly reporting, and a clearer foundation for cash flow decisions.
heading: Spend less time chasing records. Know what you’re reviewing.
intro: Late reports and scattered bank files pull you away from customers. 2ndCFO starts with imported bank and card records, consistent categories, and source transactions you can review. Use that foundation to understand spending and identify missing information. Any ongoing bookkeeping service, reconciliation, monthly close, and reporting schedule must be confirmed separately; importing transactions alone does not complete your books.

sections.heading: Reliable records, then business understanding
sections.text: The product starts with bank and credit card CSV imports, retains source rows, and supports confirmed categorization rules and manual corrections. Analysis uses the records available for the selected period. Consistent categories make spending easier to investigate, but they do not make incomplete data complete. Confirm additional service work and its delivery schedule before relying on a report. The purpose is to reduce repeated digging and give you a clearer starting point for decisions while you focus on customers and operations.

sections.heading: Start with records you can reconcile
sections.text: A useful monthly close starts with complete source records. Bank and credit card activity needs to be matched to the ledger; transfers should not inflate revenue; loan payments need to separate principal from interest. Unexplained differences should be investigated rather than carried forward as if they were settled. Potential review topics below depend on the available data and a separately confirmed service scope.
items: Review the chart of accounts against how your business earns and spends money.
Reconcile bank and credit card balances and identify missing records.
Review receivables, payables, and transactions that need an owner's explanation.

sections.heading: Make the monthly reports useful
sections.text: Your profit and loss statement describes performance over a period. Your balance sheet shows what the business owns and owes at a point in time. Neither is a substitute for checking cash availability. Read together, these reports can reveal unpaid invoices, growing liabilities, or expenses recorded in the wrong period. The close schedule and reporting scope should reflect the condition of your records and the information you can provide.

sections.heading: Separate ongoing work from cleanup
sections.text: If prior months are unreconciled, opening balances are uncertain, or personal and business expenses are mixed, define the cleanup before assuming a routine monthly process will solve it. An initial review helps establish the periods involved, available documents, and questions for your tax preparer. Cleanup needs, software access, transaction volume, and reporting complexity all affect the proposed scope.

sections.heading: Bring the right questions to the first conversation
sections.text: Bring your accounting system name, the date of your last completed reconciliation, the number of bank and card accounts, and your most recent financial statements if available. Tell us whether you need overdue records organized, ongoing monthly support, or better visibility into collections. Do not send bank credentials or confidential client records through the contact form.

example: Illustrative example only, not a customer result: If sales rise while the bank balance falls, first check whether invoices remain unpaid, debt principal was repaid, or owners took distributions. Those movements explain different problems and should not all be called an expense increase.
faq: Does bookkeeping include tax filing?
Tax preparation and filing should be confirmed separately. Bookkeeping provides records that can support your tax preparer; it does not by itself establish a tax engagement.
Can I start with bookkeeping and add analysis later?

Start with imported records and supported transaction analysis. Discuss availability and scope for any monthly bookkeeping or additional analysis; a service engagement is not established by using the product.

title: Financial Intelligence & Business Reporting | 2ndCFO
description: Understand changes in margins, collections, cash flow, and operating performance with financial intelligence and business reporting from 2ndCFO.
heading: Know where your money goes. Understand what to ask next.
intro: You need more than a list of transactions to run a business. 2ndCFO combines bank and card records with analysis of recorded income, outflows, and category spending. Supported questions can point you to the underlying transactions. Explaining a margin change or an operating cause may require billing, payroll, or job records and your team’s context. The aim is a clearer next question and a more informed owner decision.

sections.heading: Reliable records, then business understanding
sections.text: The product starts with bank and credit card CSV imports, retains source rows, and supports confirmed categorization rules and manual corrections. Analysis uses the records available for the selected period. Consistent categories make spending easier to investigate, but they do not make incomplete data complete. Confirm additional service work and its delivery schedule before relying on a report. The purpose is to reduce repeated digging and give you a clearer starting point for decisions while you focus on customers and operations.

sections.heading: Choose measures tied to a decision
sections.text: A long dashboard can obscure the issue. Start with the decisions you actually face: whether to adjust pricing, follow up on old invoices, change the mix of work, or review staffing. Then choose a small set of measures with consistent definitions. A margin comparison is only meaningful if labor and other direct costs are classified the same way in both periods. Potential review topics below depend on the available data and a separately confirmed service scope.
items: Revenue and gross margin by service line where the underlying records support it.
Receivables aging and collection trends to distinguish sales from receipts.
Payroll and operating expense trends relative to the volume of work.
Budget versus actual results with explanations for material differences.

sections.heading: Investigate a change before acting on it
sections.text: An increase in revenue may reflect higher prices, more work, a different service mix, or a timing difference. A falling margin may come from overtime, materials, discounts, or incomplete cost entries. Analysis should test these explanations against source records and operating context rather than infer a cause from a chart alone. Your team's explanation of unusual events is part of the review.

sections.heading: Keep cash and profit in the same conversation
sections.text: A profitable month can still create a cash shortage if customer payments arrive after payroll and supplier bills. Review collections, payment obligations, and the timing of large purchases alongside the income statement. This creates a useful bridge to cash flow planning without treating an accounting profit as money already available to spend.

sections.heading: Agree on the reporting inputs and rhythm
sections.text: Useful analysis depends on reconciled books and reliable operating data. Before an engagement, discuss which systems contain invoices, labor, project costs, or time records; which comparisons matter; and how often information will be reviewed. The proposed scope should identify available measures and gaps. Do not assume every system has a direct integration or that every metric can update in real time.

example: Illustrative example only, not a customer result: If revenue grows but gross profit barely changes, compare the contribution from each service line and check whether direct labor or materials grew faster than sales. That review helps distinguish growth worth pursuing from work that needs repricing.
faq: How is this different from bookkeeping?
Bookkeeping establishes the transaction records and financial statements. Financial intelligence interprets those results alongside operating information and helps identify questions and actions.
Do I need a new software platform?
That depends on your current records and reporting needs. Discuss the available systems and data first; no particular integration or platform is assumed.

title: Fractional CFO Services & Cash Flow Planning | 2ndCFO
description: Explore fractional CFO support for cash flow forecasts, budgets, hiring scenarios, and owner decisions. Discuss planning scope with 2ndCFO.
heading: Bring a clearer financial picture to your next decision.
intro: Before hiring, buying equipment, or expanding, understand recorded spending and identify what the decision still needs. 2ndCFO’s current product supports transaction-based analysis; it does not provide a dedicated CFO or take responsibility for your finances. Forecasts and scenario models are not presented as currently available product features. Use this page to prepare a discussion about any separate advisory work, its availability, inputs, and responsibilities.

sections.heading: Reliable records, then business understanding
sections.text: The product starts with bank and credit card CSV imports, retains source rows, and supports confirmed categorization rules and manual corrections. Confirm additional service work and its delivery schedule before relying on a report. The purpose is to reduce repeated digging and give you a clearer starting point for decisions while you focus on customers and operations.

sections.heading: What a separately scoped cash forecast would require
sections.text: A practical forecast starts with available cash, expected customer receipts, payroll, supplier payments, debt obligations, and planned purchases. The timing matters as much as the totals. An invoice due next month cannot fund this week's payroll unless the business has another source of cash. Forecasts should identify assumptions about collections and spending and be revised when actual events differ. Potential review topics below depend on the available data and a separately confirmed service scope.
items: Map expected receipts and known obligations over an agreed planning period.
Compare a base case with slower collections or a softer sales period.
Identify the dates when cash could become tight and the choices available before then.

sections.heading: Questions to prepare for a hiring or investment review
sections.text: A salary is only one part of a hiring decision. Payroll taxes, benefits, equipment, ramp-up time, and supervision can affect the cost. Additional revenue may take longer to collect than it takes to incur those expenses. Scenario analysis compares the expected contribution with the cash required, including the possibility that demand or productivity falls below plan.

sections.heading: Use a budget as a working plan
sections.text: A budget turns priorities into financial assumptions: sales volume, pricing, staffing, overhead, and investment. Comparing actual results with that plan helps show where assumptions need to change. The point is not to force results to match a spreadsheet. It is to see whether an unexpected variance is temporary, a recording issue, or a reason to adjust the operating plan.

sections.heading: Define the advisory role clearly
sections.text: Discuss the decisions you need help with, who will own the forecast inputs, and how often you want to review progress. Planning support depends on the quality of the records and management's operating assumptions. Engagement scope, deliverables, and meeting frequency should be agreed before work begins. Financing approval, investment returns, tax advice, and legal advice are not implied by a planning engagement.

example: Illustrative example only, not a customer result: Before purchasing another service vehicle, compare the down payment, financing payments, insurance, staffing, and expected work. Model a slower start as well as the expected case, then examine the cash balance during the ramp-up period.
faq: When does fractional CFO support make sense?

Discuss availability when a decision needs more than historical transactions. Any advisory work, forecast ownership, review frequency, and deliverables must be confirmed separately; a full CFO role is not included.
Will a forecast guarantee enough cash?
No. A forecast is a model based on stated assumptions. It helps evaluate risks and options, and should be updated as collections, costs, and business conditions change.

title: Bookkeeping & Financial Intelligence for Law Firms | 2ndCFO
description: Financial visibility for law firms: billing, collections, work in progress, operating expenses, and partner planning. Explore 2ndCFO's approach.
heading: Focus on your clients. Understand the business behind the practice.
intro: Bank and card records help you see what your firm spends. They cannot, on their own, explain collections delays or profitability by client, matter, or practice area. 2ndCFO starts with recorded financial activity and helps frame those business questions. Additional billing, time, and cost records are needed for deeper analysis, with scope agreed before work begins.

sections.heading: Reliable records, then business understanding
sections.text: The product starts with bank and credit card CSV imports, retains source rows, and supports confirmed categorization rules and manual corrections. Analysis uses the records available for the selected period. Consistent categories make spending easier to investigate, but they do not make incomplete data complete. Confirm additional service work and its delivery schedule before relying on a report. The purpose is to reduce repeated digging and give you a clearer starting point for decisions while you focus on customers and operations.

sections.heading: Follow the path from work to payment
sections.text: For an hourly practice, recorded time can sit unbilled before it becomes an invoice, and a billed amount can remain unpaid after the work is finished. Flat-fee and contingency practices have different timing and measurement needs. Start by identifying the fee arrangements and records that describe your practice rather than applying one utilization target to every firm. Potential review topics below depend on the available data and a separately confirmed service scope.
items: Review unbilled work and the age of outstanding invoices where records are available.
Distinguish fees billed, adjustments, and cash received.
Compare collections and delivery costs by practice area when cost allocation is supportable.

sections.heading: Separate operating finances from client funds
sections.text: Client trust funds require separate handling from the firm's operating money. An operating cash review should not treat client balances as funds available for payroll or partner distributions. Discuss how your existing trust records and reconciliation responsibilities are managed. Any trust-account work requires an explicitly agreed scope with the firm; this page does not promise compliance oversight or replace guidance on professional obligations.

sections.heading: Make staffing and partner discussions more concrete
sections.text: A busy team does not automatically mean the firm should hire. Review the mix of work, billing delays, write-downs, collection timing, and the full cost of additional capacity. For partner distributions, evaluate upcoming payroll, overhead, and expected receipts instead of relying on one strong collections week. Scenario planning can help make the tradeoffs visible without assuming every billed hour will be collected.

sections.heading: Prepare for a focused discovery conversation
sections.text: Tell us the size of the practice, fee models, accounting and billing systems, and the financial question causing the most friction. A first review can establish whether the priority is bookkeeping, management reporting, or cash planning. Share system names and a general description through the contact form; do not submit privileged matter details, client names, or trust records there.

example: Illustrative example only, not a customer result: If recorded hours increase but cash receipts do not, examine whether time is awaiting billing, invoices are aging, or write-downs increased. Each stage calls for a different conversation with the people responsible for billing and collections.
faq: Can reports show practice-area profitability?
Potentially, if billing and cost records support a consistent allocation. Start by agreeing which costs can be assigned directly and how shared overhead will be treated.
Does this include legal or trust-compliance advice?
No legal advice is implied. Any bookkeeping support involving trust records must be separately scoped, with the firm's professional responsibilities clearly understood.

title: Bookkeeping & Job Cost Visibility for Specialty Contractors | 2ndCFO
description: Bookkeeping and financial analysis for specialty contractors. Understand job costs, change orders, retainage, progress billing, and cash timing.
heading: Focus on the work. Get clearer about the costs.
intro: A full project schedule does not tell you what a job earned. 2ndCFO starts with bank and card activity to help you understand recorded spending. Job margins require additional estimates, labor, supplier invoices, and billing records. Start with a usable financial foundation, then confirm what project analysis the data can support rather than assuming a bank feed can explain every job.

sections.heading: Reliable records, then business understanding
sections.text: The product starts with bank and credit card CSV imports, retains source rows, and supports confirmed categorization rules and manual corrections. Analysis uses the records available for the selected period. Consistent categories make spending easier to investigate, but they do not make incomplete data complete. Confirm additional service work and its delivery schedule before relying on a report. The purpose is to reduce repeated digging and give you a clearer starting point for decisions while you focus on customers and operations.

sections.heading: Give job costs a consistent home
sections.text: Comparing an estimate with actual costs requires a consistent way to assign labor, materials, subcontractors, and other direct costs. Missing job codes or late supplier invoices can make a project appear more profitable than it is. Establish the records needed before relying on a margin report to judge the estimating or field team. Potential review topics below depend on the available data and a separately confirmed service scope.
items: Compare estimated and recorded direct costs by job or phase where data permits.
Identify costs awaiting allocation and invoices received after a reporting cutoff.
Track the effect of approved changes separately from the original scope.
Review unpaid progress invoices and retainage separately from current cash.

sections.heading: Keep change orders and billing timing visible
sections.text: Extra work can consume labor and materials before an approved change appears in billing. A job review should distinguish proposed changes, approved scope, billed amounts, and collected receipts. This avoids treating an expectation of payment as cash already available. The accounting treatment of work in progress and revenue recognition should be coordinated with the firm's accountant based on the contracts and reporting requirements.

sections.heading: Plan for the cash demands of the next job
sections.text: A larger project may require deposits, mobilization, or a concentrated period of labor spending before the first payment. Compare that demand with obligations on current jobs and likely collection dates. Testing a delayed progress payment or a materials cost increase can reveal a financing or scheduling question while there is still time to consider options.

sections.heading: Start with the project records you have
sections.text: Bring an outline of your typical projects, billing terms, estimating process, and how time and supplier costs are assigned today. Discuss whether the immediate need is reliable books, job reporting, or a cash forecast. Useful analysis may require changes to how the team records information. We will define the proposed reporting scope around available data rather than imply that every project system connects automatically.

example: Illustrative example only, not a customer result: A job with a strong billed margin may still have unrecorded subcontractor invoices and outstanding retainage. Reviewing both the cost completeness and collection schedule gives a more useful picture than comparing invoices issued with cash spent so far.
faq: Can bookkeeping alone tell me whether a job made money?
It needs job-level records as well as reconciled accounts. Consistent cost coding and complete labor and supplier records are essential for a meaningful job comparison.
Is this the same as HVAC service-business reporting?
Project contractors often focus on estimates, progress billing, changes, and retainage. Recurring service and repair businesses may need a different view of dispatch, service mix, and seasonality.

title: Bookkeeping for HVAC, Plumbing & Electrical Businesses | 2ndCFO
description: Financial visibility for HVAC, plumbing, and electrical firms. Review service and installation margins, labor costs, collections, and seasonal cash needs.
heading: Serve your customers. Understand what the work costs.
intro: A busy service schedule can hide differences in spending and work mix. 2ndCFO brings bank and card records into a view you can use to review costs and ask business questions. Comparing service, repair, installation, or maintenance margins needs complete revenue, labor, and materials records; technician productivity and dispatch-system integrations are not assumed product features.

sections.heading: Reliable records, then business understanding
sections.text: The product starts with bank and credit card CSV imports, retains source rows, and supports confirmed categorization rules and manual corrections. Analysis uses the records available for the selected period. Consistent categories make spending easier to investigate, but they do not make incomplete data complete. Confirm additional service work and its delivery schedule before relying on a report. The purpose is to reduce repeated digging and give you a clearer starting point for decisions while you focus on customers and operations.

sections.heading: Compare work that has different economics
sections.text: An installation can bring a large invoice alongside significant equipment and labor costs. A repair visit may have a smaller invoice but different travel, diagnostic, and callback demands. Maintenance agreements add another timing pattern. Agree on service categories and cost definitions before comparing their contribution, and check that field records and accounting entries describe the same activity. Potential review topics below depend on the available data and a separately confirmed service scope.
items: Separate service, installation, and maintenance revenue where records allow.
Review direct labor, materials, and subcontracted work against the related sales.
Distinguish deposits and agreement payments from the timing of work performed.
Monitor outstanding customer invoices alongside payments to equipment suppliers.

sections.heading: Look beyond technician revenue alone
sections.text: Revenue per technician can be useful, but job mix, crew size, overtime, travel, and callbacks affect the interpretation. A high-sales period is not necessarily a high-margin period. Operational comparisons should use consistent definitions and reliable time or job records. Review exceptions with the team before treating a financial ratio as an individual performance verdict.

sections.heading: Plan for seasonality and capacity changes
sections.text: Peak demand can increase payroll and materials spending before customer cash arrives. A quieter season can leave fixed vehicle, insurance, rent, and staffing costs unchanged. A cash forecast should reflect your own collection history, expected work, supplier terms, and recurring obligations. When considering another vehicle or crew, test the ramp-up period and a lower-demand case alongside the expected results.

sections.heading: Define a practical starting point
sections.text: Tell us which trades you serve, your mix of repair and installation work, your accounting and field-service systems, and how job costs reach the books. The first priority may be monthly reconciliations, a cleaner service-line breakdown, or planning for a slow season. System compatibility, reporting frequency, and available operating data need to be confirmed in the engagement scope.

example: Illustrative example only, not a customer result: If installation revenue increases while cash tightens, compare equipment deposits, supplier payment dates, labor spending, and customer balances due. A profitable installation can still require working capital before final payment arrives.
faq: Can you compare service and installation margins?
Discuss how revenue, labor, and materials are recorded today. A reliable comparison depends on assigning those items consistently to the relevant work.
What if we also handle large construction projects?
Project work may need additional reporting for estimates, changes, progress billing, and retainage. The specialty-contractor approach can complement the service-business view.
